title: Shankara and the outcaste
word: reading the Isha in the original
hookLine: an outcaste asks Shankara what exactly should move aside
carry: the same self in every being; don't shrink away
tomorrow: a woman stood up twice to question the wisest man in the room. what did she ask?

lines: VARANASI. THE GANGA. A NARROW LANE.
cards: Varanasi, early morning, more than a thousand years ago. The young teacher Shankara walks down to bathe in the Ganga, his students around him.
In a narrow lane a man blocks the way: a chandala, an outcaste, four dogs at his heels. Shankara says what custom told him to say. Move aside.
Move aside. The man doesn't move. He asks a question instead.
Move what, sir? This body made of food, away from that body made of food? Or the awareness in me, away from the awareness in you?

teach.h: HE BOWS: THAT ONE IS MY GURU.
teach.b: In the traditional telling, Shankara stops. Then he bows, and makes five verses on the spot, each one ending: whoever sees this, outcaste or brahmin, that one is my guru. Some tellings say the man was Shiva himself.
Now a verse Shankara himself wrote a commentary on, Isha six. Yas tu sarvani bhutany atmany evanupashyati, sarvabhuteshu catmanam.

teach.h: SELF IN ALL: SHRINK FROM NONE.
teach.b: Whoever keeps seeing all beings in the self, and the self in all beings. Hear the mirror: beings, self; self, beings. Anupashyati isn't a glance.
It means keeps seeing. Then: tato na vijugupsate. From that, one shrinks from no one.
Verse seven adds: for one who sees oneness, ekatvam, what confusion, what grief?

teach.h: ATMAN: THE SAME LIGHT IN ALL.
teach.b: This is one of the biggest teachings in Hinduism: the atman, the self, is the same light in every being. Advaita teachers read it as one self in all. Devotional teachers read it as the Lord living in every heart.
Either way, the outcaste's question lands. You can't keep this verse and still flinch from a person.
Many Hindu teachers retell the story to say it plainly: no human being is untouchable. And it reaches small places too. The kid everyone scoots away from at lunch.
The man on the bus talking to nobody. The verse doesn't ask you to like everyone. It asks you to see who's there.

how: Hindu teachers often quote Isha 6 when speaking of the self in every being, and the story of Shankara and the chandala is told to children and in sermons as the day a great teacher was taught; the folded hands of namaste are a bow to the one in front of you.

games.q: what does “reading the isha in the original” mean?
o: reading the Isha's own words, and seeing the self in every being
reading the Isha's list of beings to keep away from
reading the Isha only for its stories about sages

games.q: the alley and the verse — tap the pairs.
p: the teacher told to look again
asks: move the body, or the self?
the same self in every being

s: in the story, the outcaste steps aside for Shankara
he stays put and asks a question; Shankara bows and calls him his guru.
Isha 6 runs both ways: all beings in the self, the self in all beings
beings, self; self, beings. a mirror made of word order.
the verse is only about meditation, not about how you treat people
it ends in action: tato na vijugupsate, from that one shrinks from no one.

games.q: at a cousin's wedding, a relative says the catering staff shouldn't come near the mandap. you've just heard Shankara's alley. what does Isha 6 point to?
o: the same self is in them; Shankara bowed to the man he told to move.
stay out of it; the verse is about meditation, not about people.
agree; old customs about purity come before the verse.
games.why: whoever keeps seeing the self in all beings shrinks from no one. the outcaste's question still stands: move the body, or the self?

practice: Bring to mind the people you passed today: a neighbor, a driver, someone you ignored, someone who annoyed you. For each one, say inwardly: the same self in them.
If you pray, fold your hands for each, the way Hindus do in namaste, a bow to the one in front of you. Keep going as long as the breaths allow.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Isha in the original, verse six: na vijugupsate. Whoever sees the self in every being shrinks from no one.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: na vijugupsate, one does not shrink away, the last words of Isha 6.

carryVoice: Your line: the same self in every being; don't shrink away. An outcaste taught Shankara that. See you tomorrow.
